body.statement: For the explicitly defined baseline \(\mathsf R_{\mathrm{num}}\), the retention invariant is exact: after each layer it retains every feasible complete numeric history that obeys the pins already encountered, and it never merges two distinct such histories. In the three-context separation family, after the factual and normalized-query pins through \(X_n\) have been enforced, for every \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) there is a feasible retained history with \(X_{i,B}=a_i\), because the factual, \(A\)-world, and \(B\)-world predecessor tuples are distinct and unrestricted response rows can assign their outputs independently; each history extends through the remaining pin \(Y_B=1\). Therefore \(N_{\mathrm{num}}(n)=2^n\) immediately before \(Y\). From the layer after \(T\) through that pre-\(Y\) layer, all these histories induce the same three-singleton partition and \(\mathsf C_1\) retains one accepting partition state at each layer. This is a separation only from \(\mathsf R_{\mathrm{num}}\), not from all reduced decision diagrams or compilation languages.
body.justification: The self-contained family shows that the quotient removes an exponential collection of feasible numeric histories even under eager pin propagation.
body.gap: This proposition certifies a representation separation against the displayed path-retaining baseline and makes no claim about a published implementation or a lower bound for reduced multi-valued decision diagrams.
body.consumer: Compiler designers obtain a concrete regression family for testing whether an implementation has realized partition-state compression.
